metadata.title: The Advantages of Human Evaluation of Sociomedical Question Answering Systems
metadata.journal: International Journal of Open Information Technologies

abstract: The paper presents a study on question answering systems evaluation. The purpose of the study is to determine if human evaluation is indeed necessary to qualitatively measure the performance of a sociomedical dialogue system. The study is based on the data from several natural language processing experiments conducted with a question answering dataset for inclusion of people with autism spectrum disorder and state-ofthe-art models with the Transformer architecture. The study describes model-centric experiments on generative and extractive question answering and data-centric experiments on dataset tuning. The purpose of both model- and data-centric approaches is to reach the highest F1-Score. Although F1- Score and Exact Match are well-known automated evaluation metrics for question answering, their reliability in measuring the performance of sociomedical systems, in which outputs should be not only consistent but also psychologically safe, is questionable. Considering this idea, the author of the paper experimented with human evaluation of a dialogue system for inclusion developed in the previous phase of the work. The result of the study is the analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of automated and human approaches to evaluate conversational artificial intelligence systems, in which the psychological safety of a user is essential.

The Advantages of Human Evaluation of Sociomedical
Question Answering Systems
Victoria Firsanova

Abstract
The paper presents a study on question answering systems
evaluation. The purpose of the study is to determine if human
evaluation is indeed necessary to qualitatively measure the
performance of a sociomedical dialogue system. The study is based
on the data from several natural language processing experiments
conducted with a question answering dataset for inclusion of people
with autism spectrum disorder and state-of-the-art models with the
Transformer architecture. The study describes model-centric
experiments on generative and extractive question answering and
data-centric experiments on dataset tuning. The purpose of both
model- and data-centric approaches is to reach the highest F1-Score.
Although F1-Score and Exact Match are well-known automated
evaluation metrics for question answering, their reliability in
measuring the performance of sociomedical systems, in which
outputs should be not only consistent but also psychologically safe,
is questionable. Considering this idea, the author of the paper
experimented with human evaluation of a dialogue system for
inclusion developed in the previous phase of the work. The result of
the study is the analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of
automated and human approaches to evaluate conversational
artificial intelligence systems, in which the psychological safety of a
user is essential.

key_findings.claim: Automated evaluation metrics (F1-Score and Exact Match) are insufficient for reliably measuring the performance of sociomedical QA systems where outputs must be psychologically safe, not merely factually consistent.
key_findings.context: Based on experiments with a QA dataset for autism spectrum disorder inclusion and Transformer-based models.

key_findings.claim: Human evaluation provides qualitative advantages over automated metrics for conversational AI systems in which user psychological safety is essential.
key_findings.context: Demonstrated through analysis of a dialogue system for inclusion of people with autism spectrum disorder.

key_findings.claim: Both model-centric (generative and extractive QA with Transformers) and data-centric (dataset tuning) approaches can be optimized toward highest F1-Score, but this optimization target does not capture psychologically safe response quality.
key_findings.context: F1-Score was used as the optimization objective across model- and data-centric experiments.

key_findings.claim: Human evaluation reveals dimensions of dialogue system performance — particularly psychological safety — that automated metrics such as F1-Score and Exact Match cannot capture.
key_findings.context: Comparative analysis of automated vs. human evaluation approaches for sociomedical dialogue systems.

llm_extraction.methods_summary: The study conducted NLP experiments using a question answering dataset focused on inclusion of people with autism spectrum disorder. Two experimental paradigms were employed: (1) model-centric experiments testing generative and extractive QA with state-of-the-art Transformer architectures (including BERT, DistilBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, GPT-2), optimizing for F1-Score; and (2) data-centric experiments involving dataset tuning to improve automated metric performance. Subsequently, human evaluation was applied to a dialogue system for inclusion developed in a prior phase of the work. Results from automated and human evaluation approaches were compared qualitatively to identify the advantages and disadvantages of each.
llm_extraction.limitations: The paper content available is primarily abstract-level; full experimental details, participant counts for human evaluation, inter-annotator agreement, and quantitative comparisons between human and automated evaluation scores are not reported in the provided text. The study appears to be single-author and focused on a single domain (autism spectrum disorder inclusion), limiting generalizability. No statistical testing of human vs. automated evaluation differences is described. The human evaluation methodology (number of annotators, criteria, scale) is not detailed in the available content.

relationships.description: The study builds on SQuAD-style QA evaluation frameworks but argues they are insufficient for sociomedical contexts requiring psychological safety.
Uses BERT-based Transformer architectures as model-centric baselines in the QA experiments.
DistilBERT is included among the Transformer models evaluated in the model-centric experiments.
Engages with adversarial human annotation for reading comprehension, contextualizing the role of human involvement in QA system evaluation.

methodology_details.approach: Comparative evaluation study combining model-centric (generative and extractive QA with Transformer architectures) and data-centric (dataset tuning) NLP experiments, followed by human evaluation of a sociomedical dialogue system for autism spectrum disorder inclusion.
datasets: Custom QA dataset for inclusion of people with autism spectrum disorder
methodology_details.reproducibility_notes: Full experimental details, model configurations, and human evaluation protocols are not fully described in the available text; reproducibility cannot be assessed from the abstract alone.
